description: We are a passionate team of innovators, storytellers, designers, and developers inspired by space exploration, science, and technology. Our goal is to transform NASA’s forgotten space hardware into engaging stories through interactive websites, games, and educational experiences. We combine creativity, research, coding, and design to make space
summary: Astromind is an illustrated, interactive educational journey that highlights the instruments NASA has deployed on the Moon and Mars. Students choose an astronaut, select a destination, and get acquainted with a real-life piece of equipment—such as the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Mars Pathfinder’s Sojourner, or the Opportunity rover. Each story explains why the instrument was sent, how it functioned, and the scientific discoveries it enabled. Short quizzes reinforce these findings, providing detailed explanations for each answer rather than just indicating whether it is correct or incorrect. This approach transforms scattered archives and technical reports into a narrative that is easily accessible to school-aged students. Designed for a mission duration of approximately 90 Martian days, the Opportunity rover continued its exploration for nearly 15 years, uncovering evidence of ancient water. Sojourner demonstrated that robots could navigate the Martian surface, while the Lunar Roving Vehicle allowed astronauts to conduct field science far from their lander. Our primary prototype is an interactive Figma design, supported by a companion GitHub Pages site and a pitch video. The core message is this: while a mission may come to an end, its discoveries live on.
details:
What it does. ASTROMIND is a story-driven learning adventure about NASA hardware left on other worlds. The learner chooses an astronaut, picks the Moon or Mars, and meets a machine whose purpose, engineering, and discoveries are explained in plain language. Each chapter ends with a quiz. The quiz gives feedback that explains why the answer matters.

Machines featured. The Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle (Moon) showed why mobility matters for field science. Sojourner (Mars Pathfinder) was the first rover to operate on Mars. Opportunity (Mars Exploration Rover) was designed for about 90 Martian days and operated for nearly 15 years, finding evidence of ancient water.

Why it matters. Students usually hear about active missions. The histories of retired machines are spread across mission archives, photos, and technical reports. ASTROMIND connects the engineering of each machine to the science it produced. The goal is for learners to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers and to ask questions about real spacecraft.

How we built it. The interactive prototype is in Figma. A companion website (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) on GitHub Pages has a mission selector and a sample quiz. Mission content comes from NASA’s public mission pages. The 240-second pitch video combines original footage with AI-generated clips (labelled below).

Creativity. The story is told from the point of view of the machines (“Every machine has a story”), and the astronaut-selection and mission-map structure turns reading into play.

Current status and honesty note. The Figma prototype is the main deliverable. Live NASA API integration (NASA Image and Video Library, Moon/Mars Trek, PDS) is planned but not yet connected. Accessibility improvements and student testing are future work.
